1.modern-en: Dionysus opens the play standing before the palace of Thebes, announcing himself as the son of Zeus and the dead Semele. He explains why he has come to Thebes — to punish those who denied his divine birth and to establish his worship — then summons his Chorus of eastern women and departs toward Mount Cithaeron.

5.modern-en: Dionysus is brought before Pentheus in chains but shows no fear, remaining calm and almost playful while the king interrogates him. He warns Pentheus repeatedly that he is warring against a god and that his imprisonment will not hold, while hinting that his release is already certain.

6.modern-en: Dionysus speaks as a disembodied voice from within the palace, calling his Maenads to courage and commanding the earthquake that shakes Pentheus's castle. He then walks out unbound, having mocked the king by letting him chain a bull instead, while Semele's tomb blazes with divine fire.

7.modern-en: Dionysus calmly recounts how he escaped from the stables and made Pentheus chase shadows, then turns his attention to the Messenger's report of the Maenads on the mountain. He begins to subtly manipulate Pentheus, planting the desire to see the women — the first step of the trap closing around the king.

9.modern-en: Dionysus dresses Pentheus in women's robes and a wig, steadily deepening the king's trance of divine madness. He grooms and flatters him, guiding him to walk through Thebes in full view, all while speaking aside to the Chorus that Pentheus is walking toward his death and his mother's hands.

11.modern-en: Dionysus's voice from the sky calls the Maenads to see and destroy their hidden spy, triggering the killing of Pentheus. At the play's end he appears in his divine form to pronounce judgment on Cadmus and Agave, vindicating himself and ordering their exile — his punishment delivered, his godhood at last forced upon Thebes.

3.modern-en: Pentheus storms in from a journey, furious at reports of women abandoning their homes for Bacchic rites on the mountain. He mocks and threatens Tiresias and Cadmus for joining the worship, orders the destruction of Tiresias's shrine, and commands soldiers to find and imprison the foreign stranger leading the cult.

5.modern-en: Pentheus interrogates the captured Dionysus, mocking his appearance and dismissing his claims of divine authority. He strips Dionysus of his wand and curls, orders him imprisoned in the stables, and rejects the Messenger's awe-filled report of the women's miracles — vowing instead to march his army against the Maenads.

7.modern-en: Pentheus begins to crack: after Dionysus escapes captivity, the king's resolve wavers and he is caught by the god's subtle suggestion that he could spy on the women from hiding. By the end of the scene he agrees to dress in women's clothes and be led by Dionysus to the mountain — his will no longer his own.

9.modern-en: Pentheus emerges from the palace already half-mad, seeing double suns and believing he glimpses the god as a bull. Docile and almost childlike, he lets Dionysus arrange his wig and gown, boasts of the strength he imagines he now has, and speaks of his mother and her sisters on the mountain — unknowingly anticipating his own death.

11.modern-en: Pentheus's final moments are recounted by the Messenger: perched in a pine tree by Dionysus's trick, he is spotted by the Maenads and torn apart by their bare hands. His mother leads the dismemberment, and he is briefly lucid enough to beg her to recognize him — but she does not.

epithet.en: Mother of Pentheus, daughter of Cadmus

7.modern-en: Agave is not on stage but is vividly described by the Messenger: she leads one of the three bands of Maenads on Mount Cithaeron, rises from sleep at the god's cry, and later leads the frenzied attack on the herdsmen — her supernatural strength evident as she tears a live steer apart with her bare hands.

11.modern-en: Agave enters triumphant, still possessed by Bacchic madness, carrying what she believes is a lion's head on her thyrsus — it is her son Pentheus. Through a painful exchange with Cadmus, her mind clears and the full horror of what she has done falls on her; she collapses in grief, confesses her sin to Dionysus, and is finally sent into exile.

epithet.en: Founder of Thebes, grandfather of Pentheus

3.modern-en: Cadmus arrives from the castle already dressed in Bacchic robes, ready to join Tiresias in worshipping Dionysus. He warmly supports the god — partly out of genuine belief, partly for dynastic pride — and implores his grandson Pentheus to honor the new cult, warning him of Actaeon's fate as an example of what happens to those who defy the gods.

11.modern-en: Cadmus returns from the mountains carrying what can be gathered of Pentheus's dismembered body. He tenderly helps Agave recover her sanity, forcing her to look at what she holds, then mourns the destruction of his entire line. When Dionysus pronounces judgment, Cadmus accepts his fate — transformation into a serpent and exile — with grief-stricken dignity.

3.modern-en: Tiresias arrives at the palace already wearing the Bacchic fawn-skin and ivy, inviting Cadmus to join him in the mountain rites. When Pentheus attacks them both, Tiresias delivers a long and reasoned defense of Dionysus's divine power — explaining the god's role alongside Demeter in sustaining human life — and ends with a sharp warning that Pentheus's blind arrogance will bring catastrophe.

2.modern-en: The Chorus of fifteen eastern women steals onto the stage at dawn, singing a hymn of ecstatic devotion to Dionysus — celebrating his miraculous birth from Zeus's thigh, the joy of Bacchic rites on the mountain, and the blessedness of those who open their hearts to the god.

4.modern-en: The Chorus sings in defense of Dionysus and against Pentheus's arrogant refusal, praising the quiet wisdom of those who live simply and do not war against heaven, and longing for a land of peace and holiness far from the king's rage.

6.modern-en: The Chorus calls out in terror and prayer as the prison shakes, then hears Dionysus's voice from within the palace commanding the earthquake. When the god walks out free, they fall to the ground in awe and joy before rising to greet him.

8.modern-en: The Chorus sings of the slow but certain justice of the gods, contrasting Pentheus's proud violence with the quiet happiness of those who live within divine law. The ode ends with a prayer for Justice to come with her sword against the tyrant.

10.modern-en: The Chorus calls on the hounds of madness to drive Pentheus to his destruction, and summons Justice to strike him down. They invoke Dionysus to appear as bull, snake, or lion and laugh as his quarry walks into the trap.

11.modern-en: The Chorus reacts to the Messenger's news of Pentheus's death with fierce, complicated joy — relief at their own freedom but horror at the sight of Agave. They close the play with the ancient Greek reflection that the ends men look for do not come, and unexpected paths open where no one thought.

7.modern-en: A herdsman from the mountain arrives to report the extraordinary deeds of the Maenads: milk, wine, and honey springing from the earth at their touch; the women sleeping in chaste purity; and then the terrifying rampage of tearing cattle apart, raiding villages, and repelling armed men with nothing but their wands. He urges Pentheus to receive the god.

11.modern-en: A second messenger, one of Pentheus's own men who accompanied him to the mountain, returns pale and shaken to report the king's death: how Dionysus bent a pine tree down, placed Pentheus in its branches, and then called the Maenads to see and destroy their spy — culminating in Agave leading the dismemberment with her bare hands.

5.modern-en: The soldier in command of Pentheus's guard brings Dionysus in chained, but is clearly unnerved: he reports that the prisoner came without resistance, even laughed, and that the imprisoned women escaped their chains by apparent miracle. He half-apologizes to Dionysus for binding him.
